name: Costa Rica
tagline: Rainforest, volcanoes and two coasts, with some of the most accessible wildlife in the world.
cardDescription: A small country with huge biodiversity: cloud forests, volcanoes, wildlife, surf beaches and a pura vida pace.
metaDescription: A complete Costa Rica travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, from Arenal and Monteverde to Manuel Antonio, Tortuguero and Corcovado, with practical tips, a two-week itinerary and costs.

image.alt: Arenal Volcano rising above green rainforest

intro: Costa Rica is a small country in Central America, but it holds about five percent of the planet's biodiversity. Cloud forests, volcanoes, rainforest canals, dry forests and two oceans lie within a few hours of each other, and roughly a quarter of the land is protected.

The country has no army, a long tradition of democracy and conservation, and a laid-back philosophy known as pura vida. Tourism is well developed, with eco-lodges, guided walks, canopy tours and surf schools, so it is easy to visit even for first-time travellers.

San Jose is the capital and gateway, but most visitors head straight for the volcano and hot springs at Arenal, the cloud forest at Monteverde, or the beaches of the Pacific. For wilder experiences, the Caribbean canals of Tortuguero and the remote Osa Peninsula are among the best wildlife destinations in the Americas.

practicalIntro: The essentials, current for 2026. Costa Rica is welcoming and straightforward, but check official sources before travelling.

practical.language: Spanish is the official language. English is widely spoken in tourist areas.
practical.currency: Costa Rican colon (CRC). Roughly 500-550 colones to the US dollar in recent years. US dollars are widely accepted.
practical.money: Cards are widely accepted. Carry some cash for small shops, buses and rural areas. ATMs are common in towns.
practical.visa: Many nationalities, including the US, UK, EU and Australia, can enter visa-free for up to 90 days, but you may need to show proof of onward travel. Check current rules.
practical.plugs: Type A and B (US-style), 120 V, 60 Hz. Bring an adaptor if needed.
practical.tipping: Tipping is not required, as restaurants add a 10% service charge, but extra tips are appreciated for guides and drivers.
practical.safety: Costa Rica is generally safe, but petty theft is common. Never leave valuables in cars, be careful at beaches with strong currents, and use licensed guides.
practical.connectivity: Good in towns, patchy in remote areas. SIMs from Kolbi, Movistar and Claro are inexpensive.
practical.timeZone: Central Standard Time (UTC-6) all year, with no daylight saving.

culture.intro: Costa Ricans, called Ticos, are friendly, easygoing and proud of their peaceful, green country. The phrase pura vida means pure life and is used as hello, goodbye and thank you.

tipsIntro: The things that most often catch visitors out in Costa Rica.
tips: Book hotels and tours ahead for Christmas and Easter.
Roads are slow, so allow extra time.
Bring rain gear even in the dry season.
Carry insect repellent and sun protection.
Use only licensed guides in parks.
Never leave valuables in a parked car.
Carry some cash for small places.
Check tide and currents before swimming.
